Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Aug 21, 2026

Friday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 810 words, a 3-minute read.

📈 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed up 0.4%.

  • The index ends the week down 1.4% 📉. It's up 12.1% on the year. 📈

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Robinhood Markets (+13.7%) benefited along with other crypto related stocks on broad advances for cryptocurrencies.
 
 
1 big thing: Beef's growing beef
 

Illustration: Shoshana Gordon/Axios
 

President Trump ramped up his effort to lower the price of beef today, saying he would temporarily increase imports free of tariffs — and that he had secured a commitment to have the meat sold at 25% below current market prices.

  • "As we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers, for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff," he said on Truth Social.

Zoom in: A White House official said the commitment came from foreign beef exporters and that the 25% discount would be passed along to U.S. consumers.

🏷️ Yes, but: Exporters typically do not control retail prices — retailers do — so it was not immediately clear how the president can guarantee the discounts will flow through to consumers.

  • "This short-term action allows foreign imports to fill a gap to meet domestic ground beef demand at affordable prices," the White House official said.

🐂 Friction point: A U.S. cattle industry trade group said Friday it was "disappointed" by Trump's announcement.

  • "While America's cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd," Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, said in a statement.

What's next: Trump will sign an executive order authorizing the tariff-free imports within the next two weeks, the White House official said.

2. Bitcoin's bounce
 
Data: CoinGecko; Chart: Pete Gannon/Axios

Bitcoin just had itself a week.

  • The cryptocurrency is up nearly 20% from where it was on Wednesday morning.

🤔 So are the bitcoin bulls back?

  • The jury's still out, Axios' Pete Gannon writes.

Catch up quick: Bitcoin, which had been languishing below a price of $65,000 since early June, jolted to life Wednesday morning, when the Treasury Department announced plans to step up buybacks of long-dated Treasury securities.

  • At first, it smelled of a regular old risk-on trade, with stocks moving up alongside the move in crypto.
  • But bitcoin kept on rallying as stocks fizzled, when bond yields sprung right back.

🔍 Between the lines: Treasury's apparent signal that the government would be willing to step in to fight rising yields, has revived the debasement trade — and that's been good for assets like bitcoin and gold.

  • Crypto also got a boost from Trump urging Congress to pass the Clarity Act, and from the SEC outlining new rules for issuance.

Another factor at work is a sizable short squeeze, with about $2.5 billion of bitcoin short positions liquidated over the past three days, according to CoinGlass data.

  • That means that the initial price rally has been juiced by forced buying.

🗣️ What they're saying: "I'd be cautious about calling this the end of the bear market," AdLunam market analyst Jason Fernandes told CoinDesk.

  • Without new money coming in and interest rates easing, "my concern is that [bitcoin] could run out of steam at overhead resistance," he said.
 
 
3. Other happenings
 

Citadel CEO Citadel Ken Griffin, seen here at the World Economic Forum in January, updated investors today on the assets purchased from Situational Awareness. Photo: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images
 

✂️ Citadel chief Ken Griffin told clients that the firm unwound more than 80% of the risk from the original portfolio of assets it purchased from Situational Awareness. (CNBC)

🤝 The DOJ and TikTok, along with parent company ByteDance, have reached a $400 million settlement to resolve allegations of violating children's online privacy laws. (Axios)

↪️ Tesla is recalling about 3 million vehicles in China because of doorhandle safety concerns. (Bloomberg)

4. 🏀 Double dribble
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

The NBA's ownership merry-go-round is spinning furiously, Axios' Dan Primack writes.

  • The latest: Marc Lore has agreed to sell his control stake in the NBA's Minnesota Timberwolves and the WNBA's Minnesota Lynx to billionaire investor Marc Stad at a $4.5 billion enterprise value, Axios has confirmed.
  • It comes just a week after Mark Walter agreed to sell the Los Angeles Lakers to Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger for $12.5 billion.

Zoom in: Lore, a serial entrepreneur (Diapers.com, Wonder) and former Walmart exec, gained control of the T-Wolves just last summer, after a protracted legal process.

  • Lore's partner on the deal, ex-MLB player Alex Rodriguez, will remain as part of club ownership.
  • Stad was a limited partner but now takes a more prominent role. Lore is likely to retain a small position.
